entries.title: ADDRESS REUSE
entries.body:
Address reuse refers to the practice of using the same receiving address to lock several UTXOs, sometimes within several different transactions. Bitcoins are generally locked using a cryptographic key pair that corresponds to a unique address. Since the blockchain is public, it is easy to check which addresses are associated with how many bitcoins. When the same address is reused for several payments, one can reasonably assume that all the associated UTXOs belong to the same entity. Address reuse therefore poses a problem for the user's privacy. It makes it possible to draw deterministic links between several transactions and several UTXOs, as well as to perpetuate on-chain tracing of funds. Satoshi Nakamoto already mentioned this problem in his White Paper:

> “*As an additional firewall, a new key pair could be used for each transaction to keep them unlinked to a common owner.*” - Nakamoto, S. (2008). “Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System”. Retrieved from https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.

To preserve a minimum of privacy, it is strongly advised to use each receiving address only once. For each new payment, a new address should be generated. For change outputs, a fresh address must also be used. Fortunately, thanks to deterministic and hierarchical wallets, it has become very easy to use a multitude of addresses. All the key pairs associated with a wallet can easily be regenerated from the seed. This is, incidentally, why wallet software always generates a new, different address for you when you click the “Receive” button.

entries.title: ARK ROUND
entries.body:
Periodic process at the heart of the Ark protocol by which the *Ark Service Provider* (ASP) consolidates users' VTXO transactions and anchors them on the Bitcoin blockchain. Each round produces an on-chain Ark transaction containing a covenant tree in which all the output VTXOs created during that cycle are recorded.

The operation is conceptually similar to a classic Bitcoin transaction: input VTXOs are spent and new output VTXOs are created. However, the on-chain liquidity for the outputs is advanced by the ASP. In return, users hand over their old VTXOs via *forfeit transactions*. The ASP recovers this liquidity later, when the input VTXOs expire. The atomicity between the surrender of the old VTXOs and the creation of the new ones is guaranteed by *connectors*.

Rounds take place at regular intervals, typically every 15 to 60 minutes depending on the ASP's configuration. For payments requiring immediate settlement, users can resort to OOR (*out-of-round*) payments, which bypass this delay at the cost of a different trust model.

entries.title: BITCOIN NETWORK
entries.body: Refers to the global infrastructure of the Bitcoin system. The network is made up of all the nodes (computers) that run software implementing the Bitcoin protocol and that connect to their peers. Each node communicates peer-to-peer with the other nodes in order to download and verify the blockchain, to verify and relay new blocks, and to verify and relay new transactions.

entries.title: BLOCK REWARD
entries.body:
The total bitcoins collected by a miner when they find a valid block on Bitcoin. This reward is made up of two elements: the block subsidy and the transaction fees. The block subsidy is a fixed quantity of bitcoins that the miner can create *ex nihilo*. This quantity gradually decreases over the course of the *halvings*. The transaction fees are the cumulative fees paid by users to carry out the transactions included in the mined block. The fees are also bitcoins created by the miner, but their quantity is limited to the amount of bitcoins destroyed in the transactions. Indeed, the fee of a transaction represents the difference between the total of the *inputs* and the total of the *outputs*.

The block reward is distributed within a specific transaction called the "coinbase". The bitcoins extracted from it are automatically locked for a period of 100 blocks. This is what is called the maturity period.

entries.title: BLOCK WITHHOLDING
entries.body: An attack specific to pool mining. It is a malicious practice in which a pool participant finds a block with a valid proof of work, but does not share it with the pool. The attacker submits partial proofs of work (*shares*) to maintain the appearance of active participation, but withholds the valid proof of work, thereby depriving the pool of the rewards of the block concerned. This tactic aims to reduce the pool's earnings without gaining any direct benefit, but by affecting its profitability.

entries.title: CONSENSUS RULES
entries.body:
Fundamental rules in Bitcoin, ensuring the integrity of the system by dictating the criteria for validating transactions and blocks. These rules are shared and applied uniformly by all full nodes of the network. A transaction or a block that does not comply with the consensus rules is systematically rejected, regardless of any other consideration. For example, a transaction containing an invalid signature for one of its *inputs* can never be included in a valid block. A block containing such a transaction would itself be considered invalid by the entire network.

Consensus rules are distinct from the local policy rules applied by each node (relay policy, mempool policy, standardness rules). Local policy rules are configured individually by each node and can vary from one to another, whereas consensus rules are absolute and identical for everyone. Thus, a transaction that is valid according to the consensus rules can always be included in a block, even if it is deemed non-standard by some nodes. Conversely, a transaction that is invalid by consensus can never be confirmed, regardless of the context.

Consensus rules also form the basis on which soft forks rely: a soft fork consists of restricting the consensus rules by making invalid transactions or blocks that were previously valid. To facilitate the deployment of a soft fork, standardness rules are often used beforehand to make non-standard the types of transactions that will later be made invalid by consensus, which prevents a non-updated miner from including these transactions in a block.

entries.title: COUNTERPARTY RISK
entries.body:
The risk that a third party to whom one has entrusted funds, or with whom one has entered into an agreement, fails to meet its obligations, resulting in a financial loss. In the context of Bitcoin, this risk arises mainly when users deposit their bitcoins on centralized exchange platforms (CEX) or with other custodians.

The Bitcoin protocol was designed to eliminate the need to trust a third party. When a user holds their own private keys, they are exposed to no counterparty risk on their bitcoins. However, as soon as they entrust the custody of their funds to an entity, they depend on that entity's solvency, honesty and technical competence.

The history of Bitcoin is marked by massive losses linked to this risk: the Mt. Gox hack in 2014, the bankruptcy of QuadrigaCX in 2019 or the collapse of FTX in 2022. The Bitcoin community therefore insists on the principle of *self-custody*: personally holding one's private keys remains the only way to completely eliminate counterparty risk.

entries.title: EXTERNAL ADDRESS REUSE
entries.body:
Address reuse is said to be “external” when it occurs across several different transactions. In this configuration, external address reuse is a chain analysis heuristic that makes it possible to put forward a plausible hypothesis that all these addresses belong to the same entity.

![External reuse: the same address bc1q...xyz appears in three distinct transactions, a sign of a common owner.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/r/reutilisation-d-adresse-ext/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: FRACTIONAL RESERVES
entries.body: A principle of traditional finance whereby banks keep only a fraction of their customers' deposits as available reserves, and use the rest to grant loans and generate profits. In the context of Bitcoin, although the currency itself is not subject to bank credit creation, the concept of fractional reserve applies when an exchange platform keeps only a portion of the BTC deposited by its users, and uses the rest for other purposes. This poses a liquidity and solvency risk if all users decide to withdraw their funds simultaneously. This is notably why it is essential to hold your own bitcoins in *self-custody*.

entries.title: INTERNAL ADDRESS REUSE
entries.body:
Address reuse is said to be “internal” when it occurs within a single transaction, in both input and output. In this configuration, internal address reuse is a chain analysis heuristic that makes it possible to put forward a plausible hypothesis about the change of the transaction. Indeed, if there are two outputs and one of them uses the same receiving address as in the input, then it is likely that the second output leaves the possession of the initial user. The output with the reused address likely represents the change.

![Internal reuse: the address bc1q...xyz appears as both an input and an output, which reveals the change output.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/r/reutilisation-d-adresse-int/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: MERKLE ROOT
entries.body: Digest or "*top hash*" of a Merkle tree, which represents a summary of all the information present in the tree. A Merkle tree is a cryptographic accumulator structure, sometimes also called a "hash tree". In the context of Bitcoin, Merkle trees are used to organize the transactions in a block and to facilitate quick verification that a specific transaction is included. Thus, in Bitcoin blocks, the Merkle root is obtained by successively hashing the transactions in pairs until only a single hash remains (the Merkle root). The latter is then included in the header of the corresponding block. This hash tree is also found in UTREEXO, a structure that makes it possible to condense the nodes' UTXO set, and in the Taproot MAST.

entries.title: NOSTR RELAY
entries.body: A server that constitutes the distribution infrastructure of the Nostr protocol. A relay accepts events published by clients via WebSocket connections, stores them (temporarily or permanently) and retransmits them to subscribed clients according to query filters. Unlike a classic centralized server, a relay cannot modify the content of the events it transmits, because these are cryptographically signed by their authors. Each relay applies its own moderation, storage and access policies. There are several types of relays: public (open to all), private (restricted access), paid (requiring a subscription) and specialized (dedicated to certain types of content). A Nostr user generally connects to several relays simultaneously to guarantee redundancy and resistance to censorship.

entries.title: ONION ROUTING
entries.body:
Communication technique that consists of encapsulating a message in several successive layers of encryption, like the layers of an onion. The message travels through a series of intermediate nodes, and each node can decrypt only the layer intended for it, revealing only the identity of the next node. No intermediary knows both the sender and the final recipient of the message.

This principle is the basis of the Tor network, where internet traffic passes through several successive relays to anonymize connections. On the Lightning Network, onion routing is used to route payments: each node on the route knows only the previous node and the next node, without being able to determine the origin or destination of the payment.

entries.title: PARTITION TOLERANCE
entries.body: The ability of the Bitcoin network to remain unified and to maintain consensus among users, by maintaining connections and avoiding the separation of certain nodes from the rest of the network, despite attempts to fragment it. For a node to remain in consensus with the network, it must maintain at least one active connection with a set of peers sharing the same consensus rules.

entries.title: RACE ATTACK
entries.body: A form of double spend that exploits the propagation delay of transactions across the Bitcoin network. The attacker simultaneously sends two transactions that spend the same UTXOs: one to a merchant to pay for a good or service, and the other to an address they control. If the merchant accepts the transaction without waiting for a confirmation in a block, they risk delivering the good while it is the second transaction that ends up being confirmed by the miners. This attack therefore exclusively targets payments accepted with "zero confirmations" (*zero-conf*). To protect against it, a merchant can wait for at least one confirmation before considering the payment valid, or use double-spend detection techniques by actively monitoring the network.

entries.title: RANGEPROOFS
entries.body:
A type of zero-knowledge proof (*zero-knowledge proof*) used in *Confidential Transactions* to demonstrate that a committed amount lies within a valid range, without revealing its exact value. *Rangeproofs* prevent a user from creating negative or excessively large amounts that would allow monetary units to be generated fraudulently, while preserving the confidentiality of the transaction.

In the first implementations of *Confidential Transactions* on Liquid, *rangeproofs* relied on Borromean ring signatures (*Borromean ring signatures*). This mechanism is intended to be replaced by *Bulletproofs++*, which produce more compact proofs that are more efficient to verify.

entries.title: RAPID GOSSIP SYNC
entries.body:
A synchronization protocol for the Lightning channel graph that allows a node to catch up with the state of the network by downloading a compact snapshot from a server, rather than collecting *gossip* messages one by one through the peer-to-peer network.

An RGS server records channel announcements and updates, then computes a delta relative to the client's last synchronization. The format omits signatures and encodes data incrementally, which considerably reduces the volume transferred: a full snapshot of the graph takes up about 3.3 MB (1.5 MB compressed), a weekly synchronization about 566 KB, and a daily synchronization only 99 KB compressed.

Developed as part of LDK, this protocol targets mobile clients where bandwidth and synchronization time are limited. Route calculation remains on the client side, which preserves the user's privacy.

entries.title: RASPIBLITZ
entries.body: An *open source* project that allows you to deploy a full Bitcoin and Lightning node on a Raspberry Pi. RaspiBlitz provides a preconfigured system that includes Bitcoin Core, a Lightning implementation, and a suite of complementary tools such as a block explorer, an Electrum server, or node management interfaces.

entries.title: RAW TRANSACTION
RBF - REPLACE-BY-FEE
entries.body:
A transactional mechanism that allows the sender to replace a transaction with another one with a higher fee, in order to speed up its confirmation. If a transaction with a fee that is too low remains stuck, the sender can use *Replace-By-Fee* to increase the fee and prioritize their replacement transaction in the mempools. 

RBF is applicable as long as the transaction is in the mempools; once it is in a block, it can no longer be replaced. When initially sending, the transaction must specify that it is available to be replaced by setting the value of `nSequence` to a value lower than `0xfffffffe`. This is what is called an RBF "flag". This parameter signals the possibility of updating the transaction after it has been broadcast, which subsequently makes it possible to perform an RBF. However, it is sometimes possible to replace a transaction that has not signaled RBF. Nodes using the configuration parameter `mempoolfullrbf=1` accept this replacement even if RBF was not initially signaled.

Unlike CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*), where it is the recipient who can act to speed up the transaction, RBF (*Replace-By-Fee*) allows the sender to take the initiative to speed up their own transaction by increasing the fee.

entries.title: RECURSIVE - COVENANT
entries.body:
A recursive covenant on Bitcoin is a type of smart contract that imposes conditions not only on the current transaction, but also on the future transactions that spend the outputs of this transaction. This makes it possible to create chains of transactions where each one must comply with certain rules defined by the first one in the chain. Recursion creates a sequence of transactions where each one inherits the restrictions of its parent transaction. This would make it possible to establish complex, long-term control over how bitcoins can be spent, but it would also introduce risks to spending freedom and fungibility.

To summarize, a non-recursive covenant will be limited solely to the transaction that immediately follows the one that established the rules. Conversely, a recursive covenant will have the ability to impose specific conditions on a bitcoin indefinitely. Transactions can follow one another, but the bitcoin in question will always retain the initial conditions attached to it. Technically, the establishment of a non-recursive covenant occurs when the `scriptPubKey` of a UTXO defines restrictions on the `scriptPubKey` of the outputs of a transaction that spends said UTXO. By contrast, the establishment of a recursive covenant occurs when the `scriptPubKey` of a UTXO defines restrictions on the `scriptPubKey` of the outputs of a transaction that spends said UTXO, and of all the `scriptPubKey` that will follow the spending of this UTXO.

More generally, in computer science, what is called "recursion" is the ability of a function to call itself, which creates a sort of mise en abyme.

entries.title: REDEEM
entries.body: In the RGB protocol, within a *State Extension*, the term *Redeem* refers to the action of recovering or exercising a previously declared *Valency*. The *Valency*, as a public right recorded in the contract state, gives an authorized participant the ability to claim a specific extension of that state. This mechanism thus makes it possible to formalize the exercise of specific rights defined in the contract schema, ensuring that only the legitimately authorized party can initiate the corresponding transition and make use of the associated resources.

entries.title: REDEEMSCRIPT
entries.body: A script that defines the specific conditions that inputs must meet to unlock the funds associated with a P2SH output. In a P2SH UTXO, the `scriptPubKey` contains the hash of the `redeemScript`. When a transaction wishes to spend this UTXO as an input, it must provide the `redeemScript` in plain text that matches the hash contained in the `scriptPubKey`. The `redeemScript` is therefore given in the `scriptSig` of the input, in addition to the other elements necessary to satisfy the script's conditions, such as signatures or public keys. This encapsulated structure ensures that the details of the spending conditions remain hidden until the bitcoins are actually spent. It is notably used for Legacy P2SH multisig wallets.

entries.title: REGTEST
entries.body: A private testing environment for Bitcoin that allows developers to create a local Bitcoin network with the same basic rules as the *testnet*. Unlike the *testnet*, a *regtest* is private, meaning it is not possible to connect to it freely. Also, it offers total control over the network parameters. It notably allows rapid mining of blocks and the testing of specific scenarios. It is used for development, debugging and experimentation before implementation on the *testnet* or the *mainnet*. The bitcoins in circulation on a *regtest* have no value.

entries.title: RELAY
entries.body: In the context of proof of work on the Bitcoin network, refers to a tool whose main function is to relay the new valid blocks that have been found. A distinction is sometimes made between the role of the miner, who is involved in the entire proof-of-work process, from building the candidate block to broadcasting the validated block, and the role of the hasher, which is limited to participating in the hashing of a block without being involved in its selection or broadcast. The relay role, for its part, consists of broadcasting the new blocks found by a hasher. In the case of mining pools, this relay role is performed by the pool itself. It is this role that incidentally gives it a lot of power over individual hashers. The term "relayer" can also refer to the person or entity that operates a relay.

entries.title: RENDEZ-VOUS ROUTING
entries.body:
A Lightning routing technique designed to protect the identity of the recipient of a payment. In classic routing, the sender builds the entire route and therefore knows the final node. With *rendez-vous routing*, the recipient pre-builds an encrypted route segment from an intermediate node (the *rendez-vous point*) to themselves, and passes this segment to the sender via the invoice. The sender completes the route on their end up to the *rendez-vous point*, without ever knowing the nodes beyond it.

This approach does, however, have limitations: the sender cannot insert their own data into the portion encrypted by the recipient, and the amounts must be set in advance in the partial onion, which complicates multi-part payments. For these reasons, *rendez-vous routing* has been superseded by *blinded paths*, a more flexible technique that allows the sender to freely choose the data inserted at each hop and that is reusable with onion messages.

entries.title: REORGANIZATION
entries.body:
Refers to a phenomenon in which the blockchain undergoes a change in its structure because of the existence of competing blocks at the same height. This occurs when a portion of the chain of blocks is replaced by another chain with a greater amount of accumulated work.

These reorganizations are part of the natural functioning of Bitcoin, where different miners can find new blocks almost simultaneously, thus splitting the Bitcoin network in two. In such cases, the network can temporarily divide into competing chains. Eventually, when one of these chains accumulates more work, the other chains are abandoned by the nodes, and their blocks become what are called “stale blocks” or “orphan blocks”. This process of replacing one chain with another is the reorganization.

![Resynchronization at height 145: the 145-A chain is abandoned in favor of the 145-B branch that continues to 146.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/r/resynchronisation/assets/image-1.png)

Reorganizations can have various consequences. First, if a user had a transaction confirmed in a block that turns out to be abandoned, but that transaction is not found in the chain that ultimately prevails, then their transaction becomes unconfirmed again. This is why you are advised to always wait for at least 6 confirmations before considering a transaction truly immutable. Past a depth of 6 blocks, reorganizations are so improbable that the chance of one occurring can be considered nil.

Next, at the level of the overall system, reorganizations imply a waste of miners' computing power. Indeed, when a split occurs, some of the miners will be on chain `A`, and another part on chain `B`. If chain `B` is ultimately abandoned during a reorganization, then all the computing power deployed by miners on that chain is by definition wasted. If there are too many reorganizations on the Bitcoin network, its overall security is therefore reduced. This is notably, in part, the reason why increasing the block size or reducing the interval between each block (10 minutes) can be dangerous.

*Some bitcoiners prefer to speak of an “orphan block” to refer to a stale block. Also, even though it is an anglicism, people sometimes prefer in everyday language to speak of a “reorganization” or a “reorg” rather than a “resynchronization”.*

entries.title: REPLACEMENT CYCLING
entries.body:
An attack that exploits transaction replacement rules (RBF) to remove an unconfirmed transaction from the mempools of full nodes, without any alternative transaction taking its place. It mainly affects multi-party protocols that rely on CPFP to increase fees, such as the Lightning Network. This vulnerability was publicly disclosed in October 2023 by Antoine Riard (CVE-2023-40231 to CVE-2023-40234).

The attack unfolds in several cyclical steps. Bob broadcasts his unilateral exit transaction along with a child transaction for *fee bumping* via CPFP. Mallory responds by broadcasting her own competing exit transaction, which conflicts with Bob's since they spend the same inputs, along with a child transaction paying higher fees. Bob's transaction is replaced in the mempools. Mallory then replaces her own child transaction with a transaction unrelated to the channel, which causes her exit transaction to be evicted. The mempool then no longer contains any settlement transaction. Bob can rebroadcast, but Mallory repeats the cycle at each attempt, each iteration costing her a new UTXO or a higher fee rate.

This attack is particularly dangerous for Lightning Network HTLCs, which must be resolved within a defined time window. If the attacker prevents the victim from confirming their transaction before the deadline expires, they can appropriate the funds. Lightning Network implementations have deployed several mitigations: aggressive and frequent rebroadcasting of transactions, monitoring the local mempool to detect preimages before they are evicted, and increasing the CLTV expiry deltas (`cltv_expiry_delta`).

entries.title: REPLAY ATTACK
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, a replay attack occurs when a transaction that is valid on one blockchain is maliciously reproduced on another blockchain that shares the same transaction history. In other words, a transaction broadcast on one chain can be replicated on another without the consent of the sender of the first transaction.

Take the example of a hypothetical Bitcoin hard fork, named “*BitcoinBis*”. If you make a bitcoin payment to buy a baguette from a baker on the real Bitcoin blockchain, that same baker could replay this legitimate transaction on *BitcoinBis* to obtain the same amount of cryptocurrency on that fork, without any action on your part.

This type of attack can only occur if the blockchain splits into 2 independent chains that persist over time. Typically, this can happen in the event of a hard fork. For a replay attack to be possible, the 2 blockchains must necessarily share a common history, and the duplicated transaction must consume as inputs UTXOs created from previous transactions that took place before the two chains split, or from previous transactions that were themselves already replayed in an earlier replay attack.

More generally, in computing, a replay attack consists of intercepting and reusing valid data to deceive a system by repeating the original transmission. This can sometimes lead to identity spoofing on a network.

*In the case of a replay attack on a Bitcoin transaction, one sometimes simply speaks of a “transaction replay”.*

entries.title: REVAULT
entries.body:
An open source bitcoin custody protocol designed for organizations, developed by Wizardsardine. Revault relies on a *vault* system using presigned transactions and high-threshold multisignatures, without requiring covenants or key deletion.

The protocol formalizes the interaction between a cold wallet and day-to-day operations by allowing the delegation of funds with restriction policies: spending limits, authorized addresses, additional verifications above a certain amount. Each participant has their own *watchtowers* that monitor the network and can automatically cancel a non-compliant spending attempt by broadcasting presigned emergency transactions. In the event of a threat, all the funds can be moved to an emergency wallet by any individual participant.

The protocol was designed starting in 2019 by Kevin Loaec and Antoine Poinsot, and its first technical demonstrator was published in 2021.

entries.title: REVOKEANDACK
entries.body: A Lightning protocol message exchanged between two peers when updating the state of a channel. When a new payment is routed or an HTLC is resolved, both parties build a new commitment transaction. The `revoke_and_ack` message fulfills two simultaneous functions: it revokes the old commitment transaction by transmitting the corresponding revocation key, and it acknowledges receipt of the new state. This mechanism guarantees that at any moment, only the latest state of the channel is valid. If a peer tried to publish a revoked state, the revocation key would allow the counterparty to recover all of the funds.

entries.title: RGB
entries.body:
A decentralized and confidential smart contract system, designed to work with Bitcoin and the Lightning Network. RGB operates on a client-side validation model and separates the storage of contract state from the blockchain, so as to keep only cryptographic commitments on it. Thus, the full history of states is maintained off the chain, which allows better scalability and confidentiality. RGB thus enables the creation of complex contracts to issue tokens, NFTs, decentralized identities or DeFi solutions, directly on top of Bitcoin.

On RGB, resistance to double spending is ensured by the use of Single-use Seals, a cryptographic mechanism that takes advantage of the fact that UTXOs on Bitcoin can only be spent once. As for the authenticity of the tokens, it is guaranteed by the client-side verification of the history of states, from the creation of the contract up to its most recent state.

entries.title: RICOCHET
entries.body: A technique consisting of making several dummy transactions to oneself in order to simulate a transfer of ownership of the bitcoins. Ricochet makes it possible to blur the specificities that can compromise the fungibility of a Bitcoin coin. For example, if you perform a coinjoin, your coin coming out of the mix will be identified as such. This label of “_coin from a coinjoin_” can affect the fungibility of a UTXO. Regulated entities, such as exchange platforms, may refuse to accept a UTXO that has gone through a coinjoin, or even demand explanations from its owner, with the risk of having one's account blocked or one's funds frozen. In some cases, the platform may even report your behavior to state authorities. This is where the Ricochet method comes into play. To blur the footprint left by a coinjoin, Ricochet executes four successive transactions in which the user transfers their funds to themselves on different addresses. After this chain of transactions, the Ricochet tool finally routes the bitcoins to their final destination, such as an exchange platform. The objective is to create distance between the original coinjoin transaction and the final act of spending. In this way, chain analysis tools will think that there was likely a transfer of ownership after the coinjoin, and that it is therefore pointless to take action against the sender. The most common use case for Ricochet arises when it is necessary to conceal prior participation in a coinjoin on a UTXO, notably to avoid being the target of the AML/CFT policies of regulated platforms or of *blacklists*. The Ricochet tool is available on the Samourai Wallet wallet.

entries.title: RIOT PLATFORMS
entries.body: An American Bitcoin mining company listed on the NASDAQ under the symbol RIOT. Founded in 2000 in the biotechnology sector, it pivoted to Bitcoin mining in 2017 under the name Riot Blockchain, before being renamed Riot Platforms in 2023. The company owns and operates mining facilities in Texas and Kentucky, and is among the largest Bitcoin mining companies in the world in terms of hashrate. Riot also has engineering and manufacturing capabilities for electrical infrastructure through its subsidiary ESS Metron. The company is diversifying its activities toward hosting high-performance data centers for third-party customers.

entries.title: RIPEMD160
entries.body: Acronym of *RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest 160*, where “RACE” stands for *Research and development in Advanced Communications technologies in Europe*. It is a cryptographic hash function that generates a 160-bit digest from an arbitrary input. It is used on Bitcoin to transform a public key into a receiving address for the Legacy and SegWit v0 standards (for SegWit v1, the public key is not hashed). The process first involves applying the hash function `SHA256` to the public key, followed by applying `RIPEMD160` to the result. This combination of two distinct hash functions is known as `HASH160` in the context of Bitcoin. `RIPEMD160` is also used in deterministic and hierarchical wallets to compute key fingerprints. In particular, `HASH160` is used to compute the fingerprint of a parent key, which is then included in the metadata of an extended key (xpub, xprv...).

entries.title: RISC ZERO
entries.body: A company and open source framework specializing in the creation of general-purpose zero-knowledge proofs. RISC Zero provides a zkVM (*zero-knowledge virtual machine*) based on the RISC-V instruction set architecture, making it possible to execute arbitrary code written in common languages (Rust, C, C++) and to cryptographically prove the validity of its execution. The prover generates STARK proofs, which are then wrapped in SNARK proofs via a Groth16 circuit to reduce their size and make on-chain verification easier. Citrea uses RISC Zero's infrastructure to build its Type 2 zkEVM, which allows it to prove the validity of each batch of transactions executed on the rollup. RISC Zero also offers Boundless, a decentralized network of provers that makes it possible to outsource proof generation.

entries.title: ROAST
entries.body:
Asynchronous Schnorr threshold signature protocol, whose acronym stands for *Robust Asynchronous Schnorr Threshold signatures*. ROAST was proposed in 2022 by Tim Ruffing, Viktoria Ronge, Elliott Jin, Jonas Schneider-Bensch and Dominique Schröder. It works as a wrapper around an existing threshold signature scheme, such as FROST, to make it resistant to uncooperative participants or high network latency.

In a classic threshold scheme, a subset of signers must coordinate their responses to produce a valid signature. If some participants do not respond or attempt to disrupt the process, the signing session can be blocked. ROAST solves this problem by automatically restarting parallel signing sessions until a functioning quorum is obtained. This protocol is particularly useful for federations, such as the Liquid network federation, where it could make it possible to considerably increase the number of signers while maintaining the reliability of the signing process.

entries.title: ROBOSATS
entries.body: *Open source* exchange platform that allows buying and selling bitcoins peer-to-peer via the Lightning Network, without identity verification (KYC). RoboSats runs on Tor and uses ephemeral identities (automatically generated robots) to preserve users' anonymity. Trades rely on *hold invoices*, which serve as an escrow mechanism. Fiat currency payments are made via methods chosen between the parties (bank transfer, PayPal, etc.).

entries.title: ROLLUP
entries.body: Layer 2 (*Layer 2*) scaling solution that executes transactions outside the main chain, then publishes data and/or validity proofs on it. The principle is to group together (*roll up*) many transactions into batches processed off-chain, while periodically anchoring a cryptographic summary on the base layer so as to inherit its security guarantees. There are two main families of rollups. *Optimistic rollups* assume transactions are valid by default and require a proof only in the event of a challenge (fraud proof). *ZK rollups* (or *validity rollups*) publish with each batch a cryptographic proof (SNARK or STARK) attesting to the validity of all the transactions. The main benefit is to considerably increase transaction throughput and reduce fees, without sacrificing the security offered by the base layer. In the context of Bitcoin, projects such as Citrea or Brollups are exploring this approach by using Bitcoin as a data availability and final settlement layer.

entries.title: RPC - REMOTE PROCEDURE CALL
entries.body:
Computer protocol allowing a program to execute a procedure on another remote computer, as if it were executed locally.

Specifically in the context of Bitcoin, it is used to allow applications to interact with `bitcoind`. It can be used to execute commands on a Bitcoin node, such as sending transactions, managing wallets or accessing information about the blockchain. The security of this interaction is ensured by authentication via a `.cookie` file or credentials, so that only authorized clients can make RPC calls on the node.

entries.title: RPOW
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Reusable Proofs Of Work*". It is an electronic money system based on the transfer of tokens established on proofs of work, developed and implemented by Hal Finney in 2004. RPoW positioned itself as an improvement on the theoretical concepts of b-money and bit gold. 

Unlike the latter, RPoW actually came into being and was launched. RPoW could have taken the place that Bitcoin currently occupies. It was the most advanced electronic money project before Satoshi's invention. However, Bitcoin surpasses RPoW by solving two critical problems. First, Bitcoin introduced an automatic mining difficulty adjustment, a mechanism absent in RPoW, thus avoiding inflation due to the increase in mining capacity and the growing number of miners. Second, unlike RPoW's dependence on central servers, Bitcoin established a distributed consensus mechanism. This mechanism rests on the principle that nodes synchronize on the chain with the most accumulated work, thus eliminating the need for known servers. RPoW never received the support necessary to emerge and be adopted by the general public.

Unlike b-money and bit gold, Satoshi Nakamoto never cited RPoW, even though this system was surely the one that most resembled their invention.

entries.title: RSK
entries.body:
Bitcoin *sidechain* designed for the execution of *smart contracts* compatible with Ethereum. Initially known as Rootstock, this *sidechain* was renamed RSK before gradually reverting to the name Rootstock.

Launched in January 2018, RSK operates as a sidechain attached to Bitcoin through a *two-way peg* mechanism, which makes it possible to transfer bitcoins to the *sidechain* in the form of RBTC, tokens pegged 1:1 to bitcoin.

RSK uses *merged mining*: Bitcoin miners can simultaneously secure the RSK *sidechain* without requiring additional computing power. The objective is to extend Bitcoin's functionality through a Turing-complete programmable layer, while taking advantage of the security of Bitcoin's proof of work.

entries.title: RSMPPS
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Recent Shared Maximum Pay Per Share*". It is a method for calculating miners' remuneration in the context of mining pools. RSMPPS is similar to SMPPS, but with priority given to miners who have contributed recently.

This method aims to reward current contributions by increasing the value of shares submitted in the most recent mining rounds, in order to favor miners who remain active and loyal.

entries.title: RTL - RIDE THE LIGHTNING
entries.body:
*Open source* web interface for managing a Lightning node through a browser. RTL offers a graphical dashboard for common operations: opening and closing channels, sending and receiving payments, managing liquidity, viewing routed payments and monitoring the node.

RTL is compatible with the three main Lightning implementations: LND, Core Lightning (CLN) and Eclair. It connects to the node's API and provides a unified interface regardless of the underlying implementation.

This tool is often deployed on *node-in-a-box* solutions such as Umbrel or Start9, which makes it accessible to users who do not wish to interact via the command line. RTL is developed by Shahana Farooqui and distributed under the MIT license.

entries.title: RUNES
entries.body: Protocol developed by the same team as Ordinals that allows the use of Bitcoin transactions to etch, mint and transfer fungible digital assets other than BTC. Unlike Ordinals inscriptions, where each unit is unique, each rune is identical to the others, and therefore interchangeable, which makes it possible to create fungible cryptocurrencies distinct from BTC on Bitcoin. Runes protocol messages, called *runestones*, are stored in `OP_RETURN`.

entries.title: RUST BITCOIN
entries.body:
*Open source* library written in Rust for manipulating Bitcoin protocol data structures and messages. It makes it possible to serialize and deserialize transactions, blocks and network messages, to manage private keys, addresses and BIP-0032 derivation, or to work with PSBTs.

Rust Bitcoin is not designed for consensus validation: discrepancies, both known and unknown, exist with the Bitcoin Core reference implementation, which makes it unsuitable for a full node. It instead targets developers building wallets, explorers, analysis tools or any software that interacts with the Bitcoin network without fully validating it.

The project, released under the CC0 license (public domain), is accompanied by companion *crates* such as `bitcoin_hashes`, `secp256k1` or `miniscript`, and works in a `no-std` environment for embedded systems.

entries.title: RUST-LIGHTNING
entries.body: Lightning library developed in Rust, created by Matt Corallo, then adopted and developed by Square Crypto (now Spiral). Rust-Lightning provides an implementation of Lightning. It serves as the basis for the *Lightning Development Kit* (LDK).

entries.title: STANDARDNESS RULES
entries.body:
A subset of the mempool policy, made up of the rules adopted individually by each Bitcoin node, in addition to the consensus rules, to define the accepted format of unconfirmed transactions taken individually. More precisely, standardness rules dictate the structure of a transaction evaluated in isolation, independently of its context in the mempool. These rules are configured and executed locally by each node and can vary from one node to another. They apply exclusively to unconfirmed transactions. Thus, a node will only accept a transaction it would judge non-standard if it is already included in a valid block.

Standardness rules exist primarily for three reasons:
* Protection against DoS attacks: some transactions are more costly than others for the node to verify, and the asymmetry between the low cost of sending an unconfirmed transaction and the high cost of processing it creates a denial-of-service attack vector;
* Soft fork preparation mechanism: making a type of transaction non-standard before making it invalid by consensus via a soft fork guarantees that a non-updated miner will not include a newly invalid transaction in a block, which makes soft forks safer to deploy;
* Behavioral incentive: standardness rules can steer users toward practices that are less harmful to the network, or slightly discourage certain activities, such as the excessive storage of arbitrary data in the blockchain.

Note that the majority of nodes leave the default configurations as pre-established in Bitcoin Core, in effect producing a homogeneity of standardness rules across the network. A transaction that, although compliant with the consensus rules, does not comply with these standardness rules will have difficulty being broadcast on the network. It may nevertheless be included in a valid block if it ever reaches a miner. In practice, these transactions, described as "non-standard", are often transmitted directly to a miner through channels external to Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network. This is often the only way to confirm this type of transaction.

For example, a transaction that allocates no fee is both valid according to the consensus rules and non-standard, because Bitcoin Core's default policy for the `minRelayTxFee` parameter is `0.000001` (in BTC/kvB).

*Standardness rules are a subset of the mempool policy, which is itself a subset of the transaction relay policy, which is part of the relay policy in the broad sense. Standardness rules should therefore not be confused with the mempool policy, which is a more encompassing concept.*

entries.title: STRATEGIC BITCOIN RESERVE
entries.body: Stock of bitcoins built up by a state, an institution or a company as protection against economic instability, monetary depreciation or geopolitical risks.
